title: Grade 4 Division Word Problems: Remainders, Sharing & Grouping + Free Quiz
meta_title: Grade 4 Division Word Problems + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Solve grade 4 division word problems with confidence: sharing vs grouping, long division, and reading the remainder in context, plus a free quiz.
excerpt: The maths is rarely the hard part in Grade 4 division. The hard part is deciding what the remainder means — round up, round down, or is it the answer? Here is how to teach that, with a quick quiz to check.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
A Class 4 teacher in Pune once showed me a question that kept tripping up her strongest students: 53 children need to cross a river, each boat holds 8, so how many boats? The children worked out 53 ÷ 8 = 6 remainder 5, wrote ‘6 boats’, and moved on. But the leftover 5 children are still standing on the bank. That single blind spot — what the remainder actually means — is the heart of grade 4 division word problems, and it is what this guide sets out to fix.

By Grade 4 the long-division mechanics are usually fine. Give a child 148 ÷ 4 on paper and they will grind it out. Wrap the same sum in a story and suddenly they freeze, not because the arithmetic changed, but because the story asks them to decide something. Let me walk through the decisions that matter.

Two kinds of division stories: sharing and grouping

Every division word problem is one of two shapes, and naming them out loud helps children enormously.

Sharing (the NCERT term is partitive): you know how many groups, you want the size of each. Forty-eight laddoos shared equally among 6 cousins — how many does each cousin get? You are splitting a known total into a known number of equal parts.

Grouping (quotative): you know the size of each group, you want how many groups. Forty-eight laddoos packed into boxes of 6 — how many boxes? Same numbers, same 48 ÷ 6 = 8, but the 8 means something different: boxes, not laddoos-per-child.

The signal words give the shape away:

  • Sharing: ‘shared equally among’, ‘each child gets’, ‘split between’, ‘divided among’.
  • Grouping: ‘how many boxes’, ‘packed in bags of’, ‘seated 6 to a bench’, ‘how many teams of’.

The counter-intuitive bit: children who can label the story rarely pick the wrong operation. Most ‘division mistakes’ are really reading mistakes.

The remainder is not the answer — it depends on the story

Here is where marks are won and lost. The number after ‘remainder’ is raw data; the story decides what you do with it. There are, honestly, only four cases a Grade 4 child needs.

What the story asksDo this with the remainderExample
How many are needed (buses, boats, autos)Round UP — one extra for the leftovers53 ÷ 8 = 6 r5, so 7 boats
How many complete groups (full boxes, whole teams)Round DOWN — ignore the remainder50 ÷ 8 = 6 r2, so 6 full boxes
How many are left overThe remainder IS the answer39 ÷ 5 = 7 r4, so 4 sweets left
Equal share of money or lengthUsually divides exactly — no remainder₹175 ÷ 5 = ₹35 each

I drill this with one prompt: ‘Read the question again — does the leftover need a whole new thing, get thrown away, or is it the thing you were asked for?’ Three seconds of that beats a page of practice.

How to solve grade 4 division word problems, step by step

Once the child knows the shape and the remainder rule, the routine is short. Take: A shopkeeper packs 148 apples into trays of 4. How many full trays, and how many apples left?

Work through the long division

Set up 148 ÷ 4. Four into 14 goes 3 (that is 12), carry the 2 to make 28; four into 28 goes 7 exactly. So 148 ÷ 4 = 37, remainder 0. Thirty-seven full trays, none left over. Change the total to 150 and you get 37 remainder 2 — still 37 full trays, with 2 apples on the side.

Notice the answer is written in the story’s own words — ‘37 trays’, not a bare ‘37’. Teaching children to re-attach the unit is what makes them re-read and catch a wrong remainder decision.

Multi-step problems: two divisions, or a times-then-divide

Grade 4 word problems often hide a first step. Three classrooms have 24 students each. They are seated 6 to a bench. How many benches are needed? You cannot divide yet — first find the total, 3 × 24 = 72, then divide, 72 ÷ 6 = 12 benches. The trap is diving straight into 24 ÷ 6.

My rule for these: underline every number, then ask ‘what do I know, and what is the very first thing I can work out?’ Solve that, write it down as a labelled result, and the problem shrinks to a plain one-step division. Most Grade 4 multi-step questions are just a small question stacked on top of a division.

A short weekly routine that works

Ten focused minutes a day beats a marathon on Sunday. Two days on naming sharing-versus-grouping stories, two days on the remainder-decision table above, one day on clean long division of 2- and 3-digit numbers by a single digit, and the weekend on mixed problems where the child has to choose for themselves. That choosing is where real understanding shows.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The short quiz below covers exactly what we have looked at — sharing and grouping, long division, and reading the remainder in context. Let your child attempt all eight, then read the explanations together for any they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet in the box at the end gives 100 graded division word problems with a full answer key.

quiz.about: Grade 4 division word problems with remainders

questions.explanation: Four into 8 is 2, four into 4 is 1, so 84 ÷ 4 = 21.

questions.q: 96 pencils are shared equally among 8 friends. How many does each friend get?
questions.explanation: This is a sharing story: 96 ÷ 8 = 12 pencils each.

questions.q: 50 students go on a trip. Each bus holds 12. How many buses are needed?
questions.explanation: 50 ÷ 12 = 4 remainder 2. The 2 leftover students still need a bus, so round up to 5 buses.

questions.q: 40 eggs are packed into boxes of 6. How many FULL boxes are there?
questions.explanation: 40 ÷ 6 = 6 remainder 4. A full box needs 6, so ignore the remainder: 6 full boxes.

questions.q: 39 sweets are shared among 5 children. How many sweets are left over?
questions.explanation: 39 ÷ 5 = 7 remainder 4. The question asks for the leftover, so the answer is the remainder, 4.

questions.q: Three boxes hold 24 mangoes each. They are repacked into bags of 8. How many bags?
questions.explanation: First find the total: 3 × 24 = 72. Then 72 ÷ 8 = 9 bags.
Six into 13 is 2 remainder 1; carry to make 12; six into 12 is 2. So 132 ÷ 6 = 22.

questions.q: ₹175 is shared equally among 5 children. How much does each child get?
questions.explanation: 175 ÷ 5 = 35, so each child gets ₹35 exactly, with nothing left over.

faq.q: What is the difference between sharing and grouping in division?
faq.a: In a sharing problem you know how many groups and want the size of each — 48 laddoos among 6 cousins. In a grouping problem you know the group size and want the number of groups — 48 laddoos in boxes of 6. Both use 48 ÷ 6 = 8, but the 8 means laddoos-per-cousin in one and boxes in the other.

faq.q: How do I know whether to round the remainder up or down?
faq.a: Read what the story is counting. If it asks how many are needed (buses, boats, autos), round up so the leftovers are covered. If it asks how many complete groups (full boxes, whole teams), round down and drop the remainder. If it asks how many are left over, the remainder itself is the answer.

faq.q: What size numbers should a Grade 4 child divide?
faq.a: Grade 4 focuses on dividing 2- and 3-digit numbers by a single-digit divisor using long division — sums like 84 ÷ 4 and 132 ÷ 6 — and reading the remainder correctly inside a word problem.

faq.q: How do I help with multi-step division problems?
faq.a: Underline every number, then ask what the very first thing you can work out is — often a multiplication or a total — and write it down with its unit. That extra step turns a scary two-part question into a simple one-step division.
